Some days, you just can't get rid of a bomb! Andrzej Wajda's "Danton" for film bros (strange... I would've thought that was "Man of Iron"), Gotham now faces its biggest foe yet by mimicking France's Years of Terror with a bald over-E-NUN-CI-A-TING muscled Robespierre acting as the film's main villain, the movie simply doubles down on its challenging political notions from "Dark Knight", going back to the diffuse reactionary politics of "Batman Begins", in which Feuillade's "Les Vampires" meets the 2008 financial crisis. In which Robespierre turns into Mussolini, of course his muscles do not get downgraded, the jumbled mass prole (Hardy) notices the zeitgeist, decides to do a bit of terrorist tactics to its nervy populace, Batsy simply moves out of retirement (taking cues from Frank Miller, aren't we Nolan?) in his caped cowl to run around the rooftops again, cat burglar (Hathaway) in tights is a double agent, for herself and later for Batsy against the muscled prole, the real danger came in the form of the French collaboratrice (Cotillard). Psychologically speaking.... there's nothing here, everyone goes thru the motions once again, Nolan, at least for this material, is too serious of a director and humorless to notice how silly it looks to have a 6ft. guy in a bat costume and a dainty cat-lady fight against a thespian-sounding prole in metallic overalls....Is this a parody of Lang's "Mabuse", now that I think about it? Politically speaking, this doubles down on all challenges that showed up in the Patriot-Act-apocalypse of the second film, Gotham's populace too mindless to realize that the state of quasi-anarchy they've put the city into has circled back to the blind following a baldy warbling despot who plans to detonate it to smithereens (Mussolini if portrayed by Sean Connery, my nightmares for tonight), literally invoking the Years of Terror with a kangaroo court with the bare minimum of fun in the returning player of Cillian Murphy and his supercillious bob (I'll admit, I missed it). The idea, the film is invoking, is that revolution brings instability, ironically circling back to a dictatorship of the proletariat, Wajda's "Danton" informs the history, but only in my memories (no haunting slo-mo of blood dripping from guillotines), the French Revolution, apparently, needed a hero in the form of Scrooge McDuck punching everyone in sight. The ending, I swear to God, is literally the scene from the '66 "Batman" movie where Adam West runs around carrying a bomb on his head so he can toss it, babies on strollers replaced with a school bus full of kids. Someone I follow said they missed Adam West, but because of the presence of the muscled baldy here, real ones actually miss Joel Schumacher.

Being totally honest, I don’t care much for Nolan’s Batman trilogy as a whole. I adore The Dark Knight , but it feels like an outlier. Batman Begins is decent, but it’s unsure of itself and I’ve never found its story or characters very engaging. And then there’s this, in my mind Nolan’s one and only truly bad movie. I skipped this one when I last rewatched these, back in 2023; it’s one I’ve never really been able to sit all the way through, nor revisit, but, after watching the new animated Knightfall film and binge-reading the comic run, now felt like the time for reassessment. Nothing’s changed. Nolan’s propulsive filmmaking keeps it far more engaging than it deserves to be, I’ll admit, and there are lots of things I do genuinely like in here — but the vast majority of this just does not work. It doesn’t work because, fundamentally, the film is utterly uninterested in its own material. It isn’t overstuffed, yet every single narrative thread feels so flimsy and undercooked, and it’s all thrown together in a way that feels incredibly clunky. Like, for example, the audience obviously needs to care about Marion Cotillard’s character in order for a lot of this to work, but it’s almost like Nolan knows we won’t care and doesn’t care to give it the focus that it needed to change that. It’s kind of baffling. Nolan having The League of Shadows as an overarching threat in this trilogy is really quite lame, but made worse by the fact the writing around it is so weak. Writing aside, though, there isn’t even good action in this one. Hans Zimmer‘s score papers over some cracks, but I can’t think of a single action sequence I had fun with. Batman’s barely even in this. What’s even worse is the actual fight choreography, and if you have more than a cursory glance at any of the background extras during big brawls, you’ll be in hysterics . On the flip side, I like Anne Hathaway’s Catwoman. Some of her best work, and perhaps the best use of her talents. I love everything Michael Caine’s Alfred and Morgan Freeman’s Lucius do. I’m always happy to see Burn Gorman, even in a bit part. And I liked that scene when Batman says “so that’s what that feels like” (which was borrowed from the Kingdom Come comics). What I wish I could say I loved is the interpretation of Bane, because I think Tom Hardy is giving a pretty perfect performance. I even like his voice, as odd as it is; this is the only on-screen Bane that captures his intimidating intelligence and also retains his ‘otherness’. The mask is great too, and I like how Bane isn’t a lone wolf and retains the menacing patience from the Knightfall run. But… it just isn’t Bane is it? He’s a League of Shadows goon with a thing for Talia al Ghul and a mask that gives him painkillers. It’s such a shame, and not because it’s inaccurate — because it’s uninteresting. Beyond that, there are just so many plot holes and distractions. Whenever I try engaging with this one on more than an absolute base level it’s so difficult to enjoy. How did Batman get back into Gotham? Why did Bane fly out to the desert prison simply to give a little speech and fly straight back again? In what world would they send *checks notes* every single police officer in the city into the sewers in a tactical operation? How are all the policemen okay when they come out of the sewers? And Matthew Modine’s character and Talia have two of the least convincing deaths in the history of film, Talia’s now infamous. And, urgh, his real name is ‘Robin’. I have a huge amount of love for his work, so I don’t mean this as an insult, but Nolan has never been a perfectionist. Nowhere is that more obvious to me than in this movie.

The Dark Knight strives to recapture the success of its predecessors, however loses its way in a juggling of returning and new ideas, alongside some poor writing choices, to craft an underwhelming final entry to its beloved series. Suffering from a bloated story, the writers overstuffed the film with too many characters, subplots and storylines to dedicate any significant attention to any idea, leaving a serving of underbaked ideas to comprise the runtime. This leaves the film feeling particularly scattered, due to lack of focus, time that could have been spent fine tuning the significantly weaker ideas. Plot points like the entire police department of Gotham heading underground at once, only to be trapped or Commissioner Gordon keeping hold of a letter explaining the ending of the last film showed an immersion-breaking level of stupidity from the characters and a clear demonstration of the sheer convenience the writers fall back on to traverse between plot points, with little effort to convey the same meticulous attention to detail of The Dark Knight . The make or break for a strong Batman film for me is the execution of its rogue’s gallery, as the films hinge their stakes and tension on the threat they pose physically and psychologically to Batman and Gotham. Bane I found to be an especially weak antagonist, baring feats physical strength over any psychological power, challenging the characters firepower and strength, but nothing towards their ideals or methods. Paired with a needlessly convoluted plan and backstory, his character traded good writing for a portfolio of feats, making a character occupying so much of the screen time, underwhelming and forgettable. This plan ultimately loses stakes off the decision to reduce the citizens of Gotham to a faceless, collective mass, than active participants in the story’s outcome. Rather exhaustingly, The Dark Knight Rises repeats my biggest issues with the handling of The Scarecrow in Batman Begins , being given no satisfying defeat, simply being replaced by a last minute twist villain in the third act, leaving Bane’s buildup with no payoff, and the new antagonist little screen time to establish themselves as a significant threat. When culminating his shallow presence when executing such a convoluted plan, undermined by his replacement and mishandling of the people he’s directing his plan at, Bane lacked any real impact on me, making  questionable aspects, like his comical voice all the more apparent. The Dark Knight Rises was a particularly polarising watch for me, coming off the heels of one of the greatest superhero films of all time, it obviously had big shoes to fill, but the sheer buildup of lacking writing ranged from boring to sift through, to generally frustrating, culminating in a conclusion that ended lower than it started. This was disappointing to me, as the cast still carried the same enthusiasm as before, with the directing and score continuing the momentum of before, however the greater attributes were structured around a film showing just how far the dark knight can fall.

The Dark Knight Rises me pareció un cierre muy sólido para la trilogía. Lo que más me gustó fue Bane, la evolución de Bruce Wayne y la forma en que la película aborda temas más maduros. Tom Hardy hace un gran trabajo como Bane y logra que el personaje se sienta como una verdadera amenaza para Batman. También me gustó mucho la actuación de Michael Caine como Alfred, especialmente en los momentos más emocionales de la historia. Mi escena favorita fue cuando Bruce logra escapar de la prisión escalando el muro. Es un momento muy inspirador y representa perfectamente el crecimiento del personaje. El final me gustó bastante; aunque fue un poco difícil de procesar al principio, creo que fue una conclusión adecuada para la historia de Bruce Wayne. No llega al nivel de The Dark Knight, pero aún así, es una película que volvería a ver sin problema y que cierra la trilogía de una forma muy satisfactoria. Algo que hace especial a esta película es la forma en que Christopher Nolan utilizó cámaras IMAX para muchas de las escenas más importantes. Esto permitió mostrar Gotham, las persecuciones y las secuencias de acción con una escala impresionante que todavía hoy se siente espectacular. Además, Nolan intentó evitar el uso excesivo de CGI, prefiriendo efectos prácticos siempre que fuera posible. Gracias a esto, muchas escenas conservan una sensación de realismo que las hace envejecer mejor que otras películas de superhéroes de la misma época. Esa combinación entre IMAX, efectos prácticos y una dirección muy cuidada es una de las razones por las que la trilogía sigue siendo tan recordada.

Definitivamente, os estadunidenses possuem uma forte cultura do Armagedom. Ou mais ainda – um verdadeiro culto ao Armagedom. Tudo é o fim do mundo, seja na guerra, num prédio sitiado por terroristas ou numa briga de casal. E os recentes filmes do Batman, por conta da envergadura, extrapolam ainda mais tal culto, aumentando o volume, as fagulhas e o sofrimento aparente. Sem desmerecer as qualidades do filme, temos sempre uma corrida contra o relógio para salvar dezenas, milhares ou milhões. Ou tão somente o filho de Jim Gordon – um dos motivos, na minha opinião, que fazem do segundo filme o melhor da série. O outro motivo, tão ou mais importante, é a presença do Coringa. Afinal, não existe Bane capaz de superar tal personagem. Dito tudo isso, “Batman - O Cavaleiro das Trevas Ressurge” é um final muito digno para a trilogia (sempre trilogias!). Amarra as pontas e nos entrega um Batman no limite da amargura. E que precisa penar e perder para aprender a se reerguer e até mesmo passar o bastão, por quê não? Para quebrar este herói, inclusive fisicamente, Bane é o vilão apropriado. E para mostrar que existe mais do que uma Rachel Dawes na vida, nada melhor do uma Mulher-Gato. Hardy e Hathaway estão muito bem. O primeiro, limitado a olhares, gestuais e mudanças de entonação, faz muito só com olhares, gestuais e mudanças de entonação. A segunda, limitada a nada, flui, literalmente, entre vários mundos, sem nunca deixar de flertar com Bruce e com Batman. Estabelecer esta conexão entre a vilã-não-tão-vilã e o herói era fundamental, e o filme faz isso a contento. Como sempre, a trama trabalha de forma coerente seus muitos coadjuvantes, valorizando mais uma vez Alfred, Gordon e Fox. E a importância de John Blake (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) não deve ser esquecida. Muitas vezes o filme é quase só dele. Nolan também sabe bem criar cenas de ação que não são só computação. Têm ritmo, dinâmica e uma tensão sempre bem engendrada. Às vezes a mão pesa e surgem alguns exageros, mas a gente releva pelo todo. Afinal, várias das hipérboles são também os pontos de conexão com os quadrinhos. Isso porque, por mais que digam que estas histórias do Batman são baseadas na realidade, elementos como o Poço, as explicações vilanescas ou o aprisionamento dos policiais nos subterrâneos são simplistas demais se não fosse esta uma história de super-herói. Sem falar que qualquer um conheça um mínimo de Batman sacou cedo demais o principal “twist” da trama. E mesmo quem não conhecia poderia pegar rapidinho, bastando apenas ouvir com cuidado alguns diálogos (por vezes comprometidos pela péssima legendagem). Vale dizer também que o filme conta com a pior cena de “morte-de-pessoa-à-beira-da-morte” de toda história do cinema. Uma péssima interpretação de alguém que não é usualmente ruim assim. Mesmo com defeitos, o filme é um digno fechamento da série, como eu já disse, sendo equivalente a “Batman Begins”. O que não é pouco, já que “Batman - O Cavaleiro das Trevas” situa-se num patamar muito acima e dificilmente seria batido...

If you had Bruce out of commission but still hiding in Gotham, you could keep the focus within the city, and we might get more room to explore the ramifications of Bane’s occupation (it’s hinted at, but if this really is a “no but really eat the rich” populist revolt, think there needs to be a few more scenes conveying this, otherwise it all feels a bit empty). It’s a Batman movie without a lot of Batman, which I think could be alleviated a bit if Bruce at least sees/experiences all of it firsthand. -in a weird way, this rewatch made Reeves’ Batman look a lot better by comparison, despite suffering from a similar level of glut. Reeves going full noir/graphic novel feels downright refreshing after Nolan seemed to almost get tired of his own grounded take on the character. -it’s interesting how this feels like Nolan’s last formally conventional movie. From this point on, all of his movies play with time and structure, nonlinear narratives and interwoven temporalities, etc. After really finding the juice in this area with Inception, it’s easy to wonder if he felt burdened (re: bored) by the straightforward nature of this one. -to that point: a lot’s been speculated about Nolan’s seemingly recent fascination with Great Men™️ who regret their big game changing innovation, and, you know, what that might say about him. Despite not always loving the “every movie’s about the director” framing (probably true, but can invite simplistic readings), Nolan’s fixations present biographical lenses too obvious to ignore. -The bummer reading of this for Nolan is probably the real-world tragedies completely out of his control that he nonetheless might feel guilt about by association, from Ledger’s death to the DKR shooting (to be clear: he shouldn’t feel any guilt about either, but could understand from a human perspective how it’d be hard not to). -BUT my less-bummer theory is that, if Nolan’s working through some kind of artistic regret, it might be the way his work—his creative fascinations and how successful early on they were—became misinterpreted by others as his version of cinematic dogma. -whatever you think of Nolan’s “take” on Batman+superhero movies in general, at the time it felt groundbreaking, particularly his grounding of a fantastical, mythical genre with a sense of real-world stakes, logical narrative causes+effects, etc. (evoking his later take on the Odyssey). But I’ve never gotten the sense that Nolan thinks this is the end-all-be-all approach to cinematic storytelling, merely this was his approach to finding interest within the material. -I was struck watching Nolan’s criterion closet video recently when he picked Lost Highway, an incredibly un-Nolan movie in many ways. He explains that he didn’t enjoy the movie on first watch, yet on rewatches and thinking through it, he came to love Lynch’s ability to visually show illogical dream logic onscreen. For a guy that loves logic-based puzzle stories grounded in high-stakes spectacle, I thought it was telling to pick something that’s nearly the opposite. -all this to say: I think Nolan’s an appreciator of all kinds of cinematic language and storytelling approaches, not merely his own. And the longer his career goes on, the more he seems intent on playing with form (think his critics would say rather rudimentarily, but still). So I wonder if his “big regret” (if he does have one), is people deciding his “realist” approach was “best”, and not one way among many to tell a compelling cinematic story. -TLDR: Hathaway rocks, Bane voice good, etc.

Nolan concludes his reimagining of the Batman myth with a sumptuous film that pays homage to the war movie genre, presenting a clash that is no longer merely one of ideals but between actual factions in a desperate battle to save not only Batman’s soul— who is now more weary and battered than ever and must rediscover the motivation to fight— but also to save the very essence of the motivation that drives him to act: his city. Gotham City takes center stage more than ever, at the mercy of Bane, a ruthless villain masterfully portrayed by Tom Hardy, accompanied by a supremely convincing Catwoman played by Anne Hathaway. Here, Nolan consciously chooses to remove the protagonist for long part during the second act in order to tear him down and rebuild him in one of the most powerful and emotional scenes in Nolan’s filmography. The direction is, as always, extremely elegant and delivers thrilling fight sequences. The film’s flaws all lie in Marion Cotillard’s character, who is given a somewhat clumsy plot twist that fails to provide a fitting payoff for Bane’s character—who, in fact, deserved something better. But Nolan makes up for it with a marvelous ending that elevates Batman to the status of a true legend and expresses boundless love for the character.

The Dark Knight Rises is a wonderful end to a masterfully crafted trilogy. This is the first Chris Nolan Batman film I ever saw. I went to the theater with my buddies to watch this with no context on the rest of the series, and to be honest I can’t really tell you how I felt about it at the time, but I probably thought it was cool. As the years have gone on, and I’ve watched this trilogy of movies many times, I’ve always really, really loved The Dark Knight Rises. And with this analytical rewatch, the reasons I like it are kind of hypocritical. If you compare the things that I don’t like about The Dark Knight, but like about The Dark Knight Rises, you’ll see a lot of inconsistencies. But for whatever reason The Dark Knight Rises really, really works for me. I’m not quite sure if Christopher Nolan didn’t really wanna make a third Batman film, because there are parts of this that feel a bit phoned in, and that is something I’ve never thought of Christopher Nolan before. The first 20 minutes of this film are really choppy and out of sorts. It’s clunky. Scenes don’t really go well into each other. It’s kind of a mess, and while this was going on I was like, man he kind of phoned it in. But once you get past that part, for the next two hours and 20 minutes you get an epic conclusion to the Dark Knight trilogy. I love that this film feels somewhat like a James Bond movie. The globe-trotting, the scale, the larger-than-life villain — it just has that vibe. I actually kind of love that Batman is hardly in this film. He’s almost more of this mythical creature than a superhero. It creates this really interesting mythos and it allows for multiple times for him to come back to action, and it’s epic every time. Man, when that music swells and the Dark Knight is out — chills every single time. Tom Hardy’s performance as Bane is menacing just as much as it is kind of silly, and it totally works for me. I love the characterization of Bane. His voice is so over the top and his little one-liners are so silly, but I think it adds to the mental state of Bane. He’s just a crazy British guy who was trained by the League of Shadows and lived in a hole for his whole life. It’s awesome. Anne Hathaway — good Lord Almighty, what a Catwoman. She not only looks the part but she is so good at bullshitting people. She changes her attitude on a dime. It shows how much range she has as an actor and it’s something that’s been kind of brushed over, but she’s the best actor in this film easily. I can go on and on about the entire cast to be honest. Michael Caine, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Morgan Freeman, Gary Oldman — all are just perfectly cast, and seeing their stories come to an end is such a delight. This film had me really in awe through most of it. The scale of how many people they have in the streets of Gotham fighting, or the Batwing flying around — it all just looks so great and it’s so not half-assed. So to circle it around from the beginning of this review, the beginning of this movie is just a little janky, but this film is not half-assed. And I will say still to this day, after re-watching this whole entire trilogy, I still enjoy The Dark Knight Rises more than The Dark Knight. Thanks for listening.
